# A Flexible Density Built from Gaussian Components

A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) represents a continuous multivariate distribution
as a weighted sum of Gaussian densities. For observation $Y_i\in\mathbb R^d$,
introduce a latent component $Z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$:

$$
P(Z_i=k)=\pi_k,
\qquad
Y_i\mid Z_i=k\sim N_d(\mu_k,\Sigma_k),
$$

where $\pi_k>0$, $\sum_k\pi_k=1$, and each $\Sigma_k$ is positive definite.
Marginalizing $Z_i$ gives

$$
\boxed{p(y_i\mid\theta)
=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\phi_d(y_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k).}
$$

This model can approximate multimodal or asymmetric densities even though each
component is Gaussian. A component is a term in a probability model, however,
not automatically a real biological subtype. Density estimation, prediction,
soft clustering, and discovery of stable biological states are distinct goals.

# Start with the Target and Experimental Unit

Before fitting, specify what one row represents and what the mixture is meant to
learn. Possible targets include the marginal density of a measured profile, the
probability that a new profile belongs to an operational component, or a
component-level mean. These targets require different validation.

In an omics study, cells, spots, peaks, or reads may be nested measurements while
donors, organisms, or independently prepared specimens are the experimental
units. An iid cell-level mixture describes a pooled cell distribution only under
strong exchangeability assumptions. It does not justify donor-level treatment
inference from thousands of cells as though they were independent biological
replicates.

# Distributional Properties

The mixture mean is

$$
\mu=E(Y)=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\mu_k.
$$

The law of total variance decomposes the covariance into within- and
between-component variation:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\Sigma_k
+\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k(\mu_k-\mu)(\mu_k-\mu)^\mathsf T.
$$

Thus the covariance of the pooled data is not a typical within-component
covariance. A multimodal mixture can have the same global mean and covariance as
a single Gaussian distribution, so first and second moments alone cannot reveal
the component structure.

The posterior component probability, or responsibility, is

$$
\tau_{ik}=P(Z_i=k\mid Y_i=y_i)
=\frac{\pi_k\phi_d(y_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}
{\sum_{h=1}^K\pi_h\phi_d(y_i;\mu_h,\Sigma_h)}.
$$

A maximum-posterior hard assignment chooses $\arg\max_k\tau_{ik}$, but this
compression discards classification uncertainty. Entropy such as
$-\sum_k\tau_{ik}\log\tau_{ik}$ makes overlap visible.

# Geometry Through the Covariance Matrices

Each covariance matrix controls a component's size, orientation, and shape.
Common model families constrain these matrices:

| Covariance structure | Geometric implication | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| $\Sigma_k=\sigma^2I$ | equal spherical components | few parameters, often unrealistic |
| $\Sigma_k=\sigma_k^2I$ | spherical components of different sizes | cannot represent correlation |
| $\Sigma_k=\Sigma$ | equal ellipsoidal shape and orientation | stable but restrictive |
| diagonal $\Sigma_k$ | axis-aligned ellipsoids | assumes conditional feature independence |
| unrestricted $\Sigma_k$ | component-specific ellipsoids | flexible; needs much more information |

An unrestricted covariance has $d(d+1)/2$ parameters per component. When $d$ is
large relative to component effective sample sizes, estimates can be singular or
unstable. Feature selection, scientifically defensible dimension reduction,
parsimonious covariance parameterizations, or regularization may be necessary.
The preprocessing step becomes part of the fitted procedure and must be repeated
inside validation or resampling.

# Likelihood and EM Estimation

For independent observations, the log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\theta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\log
\left\{\sum_{k=1}^K
\pi_k\phi_d(y_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right\}.
$$

[Expectation--maximization](expectation-maximization.qmd) is commonly used to
maximize it. Starting from current parameters, its E-step computes $\tau_{ik}$.
With $N_k=\sum_i\tau_{ik}$, the unrestricted M-step is

$$
\hat\pi_k=\frac{N_k}{n},
\qquad
\hat\mu_k=\frac{\sum_i\tau_{ik}y_i}{N_k},
$$

$$
\hat\Sigma_k
=\frac{\sum_i\tau_{ik}\,
(y_i-\hat\mu_k)(y_i-\hat\mu_k)^\mathsf T}{N_k}.
$$

The updates resemble weighted Gaussian estimates, but they do not make the
observed likelihood convex. Use many dispersed starts, retain the solution with
the best valid objective rather than the first converged fit, and compare
label-invariant fitted densities. Initialization by hierarchical clustering or
$K$-means can be useful, but neither guarantees the global optimum.

# The Gaussian-mixture Likelihood Can Be Unbounded

An unconstrained GMM with $K\geq2$ has a fundamental singularity. Center one
component at an observation $y_j$ and let its covariance approach zero. The
Gaussian density at $y_j$ tends to infinity, so the likelihood can diverge even
though the resulting component is not a meaningful population.

Software may stop before the mathematical singularity because of numerical
floors, but that is an implementation guard rather than evidence that the
unconstrained MLE exists. Defensible responses include covariance constraints,
penalized likelihood, informative priors, or a simpler component family. The
choice changes the estimand and should be reported. Removing the inconvenient
observation after seeing the collapse can hide genuine tails or contamination.

# Identifiability and the Meaning of Components

Finite Gaussian mixtures are identifiable under standard conditions up to a
permutation of component labels, but this population result does not guarantee
useful finite-sample separation. Components with similar means and covariances,
tiny weights, or strong overlap can be practically weakly identified.

Because

$$
\sum_k\pi_k\phi_d(y;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)
=\sum_k\pi_{\sigma(k)}
\phi_d(y;\mu_{\sigma(k)},\Sigma_{\sigma(k)})
$$

for any permutation $\sigma$, raw component numbers have no inherent meaning.
[Identifiability and label switching](identifiability-and-label-switching.qmd)
explains invariant targets, ordering constraints, and matching across fits.
Moreover, a non-Gaussian skewed population may be approximated by several
Gaussian components. In that case, $K$ describes approximation complexity, not
the number of biological populations.

# Choosing the Number of Components

There is no universally correct criterion because “how many components?” depends
on the target.

## Information criteria

For a regular model, the Bayesian information criterion is

$$
\operatorname{BIC}=-2\ell(\hat\theta_K)+p_K\log n.
$$

Smaller BIC balances fit and parameter count and is widely used for mixtures.
Mixtures are nonregular at zero weights and coincident components, so the usual
Laplace derivation is not automatically valid. BIC remains a heuristic whose
stability should be checked, not a proof of a true number of classes.

The integrated completed likelihood adds a preference for confident separation
and therefore targets clustering more directly than density fit. It can favor a
different $K$ when overlapping components improve the density but not crisp
classification.

## Predictive validation and stability

Held-out log density assesses prediction for unseen observations. Its splits must
respect the intended generalization unit: donor-level splits are needed for
claims about new donors. Also examine whether modes, memberships, and substantive
summaries are stable across starts, bootstrap samples, preprocessing choices,
and reasonable covariance families.

A likelihood-ratio test comparing $K$ with $K+1$ does not generally have the
usual chi-squared null distribution because the extra weight is on a boundary
and component parameters are unidentified under the null. Specialized theory or
a carefully designed parametric bootstrap is required.

# Worked Example: Two Marker-defined Cell States

Suppose two standardized protein markers are measured in cells from each of
$m$ donors. A two-component GMM may represent low- and high-activation profiles.
For donor $j$, a measurement-level summary might be

$$
\hat q_j=\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}
P(Z_{ij}=\text{high}\mid y_{ij},\hat\theta).
$$

This soft proportion retains more information than counting hard assignments.
The treatment estimand could then be a contrast in donor-level $q_j$ values, or
it could be defined in a joint hierarchical model. The $m$ donors—not the
$\sum_j n_j$ cells—determine biological replication for that contrast.

Uncertainty must include fitting and classification uncertainty, not only the
binomial variation of assigned cells. A donor-level bootstrap or hierarchical
model can preserve the sampling design. If batches are confounded with treatment,
neither visually separated components nor a small within-model standard error
identifies a treatment effect.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity

| Model aspect | What to inspect | Consequence or sensitivity analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Global fit | held-out log density; predictive contours; marginal and bivariate checks | compare component families and transformations |
| Local optima | log-likelihood and invariant predictions across starts | retain distinct high-likelihood solutions |
| Overlap | responsibility entropy and classification error estimates | report soft membership; avoid overconfident labels |
| Tiny components | $\hat\pi_k$, $N_k$, and stability under resampling | test whether they represent tails, artifacts, or singular fits |
| Covariance stability | eigenvalues, condition numbers, and sensitivity to regularization | simplify or regularize the covariance structure |
| Number of components | BIC or other criteria, predictive performance, and bootstrap stability | report a plausible range when selection is unstable |
| Design dependence | donor- and batch-stratified fit and validation | add hierarchical structure or change the inferential unit |
| Biological identity | reproducible markers and external assays | call components statistical clusters until validated |

Checking only a projected scatterplot can miss misfit in other dimensions.
Conversely, apparent clusters after a visualization embedding may be induced or
exaggerated by that nonlinear preprocessing; fit and validate the probabilistic
model in a declared feature space.

# Common Misinterpretations

- **“Gaussian components require Gaussian pooled data.”** The mixture is usually
  non-Gaussian; Gaussianity is conditional on a component.
- **“The selected $K$ is the number of cell types.”** It may instead reflect
  skewness, tails, technical variation, or a useful density approximation.
- **“A hard assignment is observed truth.”** It suppresses responsibility
  uncertainty and depends on the model and loss function.
- **“Successful EM output is a valid MLE.”** The fit may be local, singular, or
  weakly identified.
- **“Many cells guarantee precise treatment inference.”** Independent donors,
  design balance, and between-donor variability determine that inference.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Finite mixture models](finite-mixture-models.qmd) gives the general latent
  mixture framework, moments, targets, and diagnostics.
- [Expectation--maximization](expectation-maximization.qmd) derives the
  lower-bound algorithm used for likelihood fitting.
- [Identifiability and label switching](identifiability-and-label-switching.qmd)
  explains why component labels require a convention or scientific anchor.
- [Multivariate normal distributions](../probability-randomness/normal-and-multivariate-normal-distributions.qmd)
  develops the component density and covariance geometry.
- [AIC, BIC, and information criteria](../regression-models/aic-bic-and-information-criteria.qmd)
  explains information criteria and the assumptions behind them.
- [Train, validation, and test-set design](../regression-models/train-validation-and-test-set-design.qmd)
  shows how validation units must match the deployment target.

GMMs are flexible density models whose components can support soft clustering,
but component count and biological class count need not agree. Covariance
structure, likelihood singularities, local optima, overlap, selection uncertainty,
and label symmetry all require explicit checks. In biological applications,
validation across independent specimens and a correct experimental unit matter
more than the number of nested measurements.
